name: root
why: CERN's data analysis framework for particle physics is real science software you can run at home.

brief.what_it_is: ROOT is a C++ data analysis framework from CERN for storing, processing, and analysing large scientific datasets, from acquisition through to publication-ready plots. It takes in event or measurement data, typically stored in ROOT's columnar file format, and produces histograms, fits, statistical models, and plots. It can be driven interactively through a C++ interpreter (Cling) or from Python via dynamic bindings, and it can run analyses in batch mode. The Homebrew formula installs a set of command-line tools alongside it, such as root, hadd, rootls, and rootcling.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a unified package that is reliable, performant, and easy to obtain, aiming to get the most scientific results per unit of human effort and computing cost. Its homepage says more than 2 exabytes are stored in ROOT files, and it was built for the Large Hadron Collider experiments.
brief.how_it_works: Cling, a C++-compliant interpreter, lets users prototype in C++ without a compile step, and its type introspection supports Python interoperability. Python bindings use the cppyy technology for on-demand, two-way C++/Python access. RDataFrame is a parallel processing framework that can use multiple cores or distributed systems to speed up analyses.

brief.install_notes: No extra hardware or accounts are needed for a local install. Per the Homebrew caveats, the thisroot.* scripts are no longer required from ROOT 6.22 on, but you still need to source the one for your shell if your scripts depend on the variables it sets. The README points to root.cern/install for installation and to root.cern/install/build_from_source for building from source. The SWAN live demo is only for CERN users.
brief.standout: It is real high-energy physics infrastructure, not a toy: the README says Exabytes of data are written in ROOT's columnar format, and the homepage notes the Higgs discovery used it. It also pairs a C++ interpreter with Python bindings, so you can prototype in either language on the same objects.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists release 6.40.04 on 27 August 2026, release 6.40.02 on 11 June 2026, and 6.40.00 on 20 May 2026, with news items dated as late as September 2026. The GitHub repo is root-project/root.
brief.caveats: Licensed under LGPL v2.1 or later. The README's SWAN live demo is labelled 'for CERN Users', so it is not open to everyone. The README gives no platform list, and building from source is a separate, larger job than installing via Homebrew. The Homebrew caveats only cover shell setup and do not describe any other first-run steps.

entry.title: ROOT
entry.tldr: CERN's C++ data analysis framework, built for the Large Hadron Collider, with an interactive C++ interpreter and Python bindings for histograms, fits and plots.
entry.deeper_look:
ROOT is a framework for storing, processing and analysing very large scientific datasets, from acquisition through to publication-ready plots. It reads event or measurement data, typically held in its own columnar file format, and produces histograms, fits, statistical models and plots. The Homebrew formula also installs a set of command-line tools, such as `root`, `hadd`, `rootls` and `rootcling`.

It was built for the Large Hadron Collider experiments. The homepage says more than 2 exabytes are stored in ROOT files, and that the Higgs discovery used it. The README frames it as a unified package that is reliable, performant and easy to obtain, aiming for the most scientific results per unit of human effort and computing cost.

The interesting part is how you drive it. Cling, a C++-compliant interpreter, lets you prototype in C++ with no compile step. Its type introspection also supports the Python bindings, which use cppyy for on-demand, two-way access between C++ and Python. You can work in either language on the same objects, or run analyses in batch mode.

RDataFrame, the parallel processing framework, can spread an analysis across multiple cores or distributed systems. In the project's words: "Exabytes of scientific data are written in columnar ROOT format." It is a way to see what a working particle-physics analysis toolchain looks like, on your own machine.
entry.install:
brew install root
# Optional since ROOT 6.22. For bash, to set the custom variables the thisroot scripts export:
. $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/bin/thisroot.sh
# No extra hardware or accounts needed. The formula pulls in many dependencies, including gcc and Python.

entry.whats_unique: It is real high-energy physics infrastructure, not a toy, and it pairs a C++ interpreter with Python bindings so you can prototype in either language on the same objects.
entry.caveats: The install is large, with a long dependency list, and the README's SWAN live demo is only for CERN users.
